nameStory: This tiny freshwater algae is named after Jacques Philippe Raymond Draparnaud, a French naturalist who studied mollusks and other small aquatic creatures in the early 1800s. The species name 'glomerata' means 'clustered' in Latin, describing how this algae forms dense, ball-like clumps in the water. It's a fitting tribute to someone who appreciated the intricate beauty of small water-dwelling organisms!
description: Draparnaldia glomerata is a freshwater green algae that forms distinctive clusters in clean streams and ponds. Unlike the plants we usually think of, this is actually a colony of microscopic cells that work together, creating visible green tufts or balls that can range from pea-sized to golf ball-sized. You'll need to look closely to spot these delicate, translucent green formations floating or attached to rocks and vegetation in the water. Each colony is made up of branching threads of cells that are too small to see individually without a magnifying glass.

idTips.label: Clustered growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms dense, rounded clumps or tufts that look like tiny green cotton balls floating in the water or attached to surfaces

idTips.label: Branching structure
idTips.description: Under close inspection with a hand lens, you can see delicate, tree-like branching patterns within each clump

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels slimy and gelatinous to the touch, like wet cotton or moss, but much more delicate and easily broken apart

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to medium green when healthy, becoming yellowish or brownish when stressed or dying

idTips.label: Water attachment
idTips.description: Often found attached to rocks, sticks, or other submerged objects, but can break free and float as loose masses

habitat: Look for Draparnaldia glomerata in clean, cool freshwater streams, ponds, and slow-moving rivers throughout New England. It prefers areas with good water quality and moderate light levels, often attaching to rocks, fallen logs, or aquatic plants in shallow areas. This algae is particularly common in spring-fed waters and mountain streams where the water stays relatively cool and unpolluted.

seasonality.spring: Most abundant and easiest to spot as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. Colonies are bright green and actively growing.
seasonality.summer: Still present but may be less noticeable as other aquatic plants become more dominant. Look in cooler, shadier parts of water bodies.
seasonality.fall: Colonies may start to break apart and become less vibrant as temperatures drop and light decreases.
seasonality.winter: Greatly reduced or dormant under ice, though some may persist in areas with flowing water that doesn't freeze completely.

funFact: This tiny algae is actually one of nature's water quality detectives - it only thrives in clean water, so finding healthy colonies of Draparnaldia is a sign that your local stream or pond has excellent water quality with low pollution levels!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other green algae masses or even young moss growing underwater. The key difference is Draparnaldia's distinctive clustered, cotton ball-like appearance and its slimy texture - remember 'Drama balls' (Draparnaldia) form dramatic round clusters, while other algae tend to form sheets or stringy masses.
contextualKnowledge: While called an 'algae,' this organism represents an ancient group that's neither plant nor animal but something in between. Many people think all slimy green stuff in water is the same, but Draparnaldia is actually quite sophisticated, with specialized cells for different functions within each colony.
compareHints: Draparnaldia glomerata forms more compact, rounded clusters compared to its relative Draparnaldia mutabilis, which tends to create looser, more sprawling formations. Both species have the characteristic branching pattern under magnification, but glomerata's 'glomerulus' or ball-like clusters are much more tightly packed and defined. If you're looking at a neat, round green puff, it's likely glomerata; if it's more of a loose, spreading mass, think mutabilis.
